title: ‘To Catch a Predator’ Host Chris Hansen Watches Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ — and He’s Not a Fan
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All September 25, 2026 7:41pm Chris Hansen Jason Mendez/Getty Images Former To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen was interviewed on his podcast Friday to give his unfiltered reaction to A24 ‘s unauthorized, dramatized film about parts of his life, Primetime , which he called overly dramatic, detached from reality, and a “fever dream” — while giving Robert Pattinson ‘s performance a “D” grade. Primetime , which opens Friday in the U.S., is set in 2006 and follows Pattinson’s fictionalized version of Hansen as the popular To Catch a Predator segment on NBC’s Dateline grows into its own primetime block on the network. On the show, Hansen blurred journalistic lines by working with law enforcement and the watchdog group Perverted Justice to intercept adult men as they arrived, unbeknownst to them, at a sting house to meet a minor they’d met online for sex. The men were typically arrested as a result. The series drew mixed reactions, with concerns about potential entrapment-law violations at the forefront of the criticism. Related Stories Movies Chris Hansen Strikes Back at 'Primetime' Movie (Again) With 'I'm Chris Hansen' Documentary Trailer Movies 'Avengers: Endgame' Returns to Box Office With $3.8M Previews as Brad Pitt, Robert Pattinson Join Fray In a brief segment produced for his video podcast, Have a Seat with Chris Hansen , the former NBC News journalist is seen exiting a Times Square AMC after viewing the film for the first time at a Thursday night screening — his first look at the indie drama since its theatrical release. He’s then asked for his first reaction to the Lance Oppenheim-directed film . “It’s hard for me to — obviously, I’m not a judge, because the character is based on me,” he said. “I think because the character is so detached from reality, from anything I’ve ever experienced then or now doing the investigations — I’m not sure what the point of it was.” The rest of the podcast episode has Hansen discussing the film, its director and Pattinson’s portrayal of him with Fox News’ Jesse Watters. Hansen railed against the movie throughout. Oppenheim has said he conceived Primetime after receiving a personalized Cameo video from the To Catch a Predator host. Hansen said on his podcast that he spoke to a mutual friend before seeing the film, and that Oppenheim told the friend it was “something to the effect of, ‘a love letter to Chris Hansen, and it gets a little weird in the storytelling.'” Hansen also flagged inaccuracies in the fictionalized version of his life — including scenes involving Jeff Zucker and Stone Phillips that he insists never happened — and said absolutely nothing in the film was close to reality. He assured viewers he’s not the ratings-obsessed figure the script conjures. His biggest gripe, he said, is that the film portrays him as an aloof parent, which he says is far from how he relates to his kids. As for Pattinson’s take on Hansen circa 2006, Hansen had few kind words. “He’s got work to do. I’m kind of the only guy that counts for this, right?” he said. Days before seeing the movie, Hansen spoke with The Hollywood Reporter ‘s Seth Abramovich about what he knew of the film. A24 hadn’t reached out to him or the production to explain the premise or ask for his input, he said. “Based upon what I’ve seen in the trailer and my understanding of what’s been written about the film, they wanted to create something much darker and way more dramatic,” he said. “I think it’s an insult to the thousands of men and women who work hard every day to protect children from predators. They’ve turned something that is very positive, very challenging and not without risk into what is essentially a horror film.” On Friday, after viewing Primetime , he doubled down with a direct swipe at Oppenheim. “You have to question the motives of not coming forward and talking to me or anybody I’ve worked closely with over the years,” he said. “They didn’t want to hear that Chris Hansen is a good guy. They didn’t want to hear that this work is important. This director had a dark image of what he wanted to do. He wanted to create a horror-like film with interesting photography, and didn’t want to hear anything else.” Hansen continues identifying and capturing potential child predators on Takedown with Chris Hansen . Earlier on Friday, Hansen’s TruBlu streaming network dropped the trailer for I’m Chris Hansen , a documentary centered around the host. THR

Written and directed by Vishal Chaturvedi and adapted from his book “Divine Detour: That Changed My Life,” the film follows Lakshman Das, a boy who leaves home after his mother dies, searching for the divine. Years of wandering and meditation later, he becomes the saint Neem Karoli Baba, known to devotees as Maharaj-ji. Shobhinaw Satyaa plays the title role opposite Chandan Anand, with Vihaan Shedge as the teenage Maharaj-ji and Anil Rastogi and Purnima Tiwari in supporting roles. Chaturvedi produced with Ragini Sona, Namrata G. Singh and Anupriya A. Nagar under his Swambhu Media Network banner. Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture “Our strategy involved taking ownership of all global territories and collaborating with the biggest local partners in each region to ensure the best possible release footprint. By leveraging the data and learnings from our previous releases like ‘Mahavatar Narsimha,’ we were able to tap into the right locations and cinema chains. This targeted approach has yielded spectacular numbers,” says Hombale Films producer Chaluve Gowda. Popular on Variety The Bengaluru banner partnered with Phars in the GCC and Prathyangara in North America, and the film opened internationally on Sept. 11. It marks a first for the company. “‘Hanuman Ansh’ is the first film outside of our own productions that we have full fledgedly distributed internationally. We truly believed in this project, as it perfectly aligns with our vision of taking Indian stories global,” Gowda says. North America leads the overseas tally, with $1.8 million from the U.S. and Canada, according to Hombale’s territory figures. Australia and New Zealand contributed $606,716 and the Gulf Cooperation Council region $577,870, with the U.K. adding $269,837. Singapore brought in $61,334 and Europe $41,171, while the rest of the world accounted for $483,006. Hombale previously backed the animated “Mahavatar Narsimha,” which went on to do more than INR300 crore ($31.3 million) in business. At home, the film has been a sleeper. Made for approximately INR2 crore ($209,000), “Hanuman Ansh” opened in India on Aug. 7 on some 250 screens through Cinépolis India. Word of mouth pushed it past 2,000 screens, and it has since grossed INR340.7 crore ($35.5 million) in seven weeks. Chaturvedi has planned the film as the first part of a trilogy. “We will always support the makers in bringing their ultimate vision to life. These are exactly the kinds of stories we want to champion as a production house, and we will continue to back creators who dare to tell such grand stories with all their heart,” Gowda says. full_text: Sep 25, 2026 6:16pm PT Scarlett Johansson Takes Break From Filming Overseas for ‘Paper Tiger’ NYFF Premiere After Skipping Cannes: ‘I’m Hallucinating’ By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest Scarlett Johansson Takes Break From Filming Overseas for ‘Paper Tiger’ NYFF Premiere After Skipping Cannes: ‘I’m Hallucinating’ 12 hours ago New York Film Festival Boss on Scoring ‘Artificial’ and ‘Behemoth’ World Premieres and Why Movies Are ‘Unavoidably Political’ 24 hours ago Paige DeSorbo on Leaving ‘Summer House’ Behind and Speaking Out About a Past Abusive Relationship: ‘Domestic Violence’ Can ‘Truly Happen to Anyone’ 3 days ago See All Getty Images A very jet-lagged Scarlett Johansson reunited with co-stars Adam Driver and Miles Teller for the New York Film Festival premiere of “ Paper Tiger ,” which kicked off the festival’s 64th edition. “I’m hallucinating,” said Johansson, who just got off a long international flight, where she’s filming another movie. “It’s 5 in the morning — which is a great time to be doing an interview on stage.” Related Stories SkyShowtime Could Be Shut Down, Warns Board of Comcast-Paramount Joint Venture “Paper Tiger” premiered in May at the Cannes Film Festival. title: International Documentary Association Calls On Israeli Government To Halt “Campaign Of Threats” Against ‘NAZA’ Directors
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew International Documentary Association Calls On Israeli Government To Halt “Campaign Of Threats” Against ‘NAZA’ Directors Producers Ross Kauffman, Sarah Sarandos, Scott Veltri Board ‘They Were Good Dogs,’ Lily Blavin Exposé On Beagles Used For Research Trailer Released For ‘Musk,’ Damning Doc Portraying World’s Richest Man As Power-Hungry Cretin View All September 25, 2026 5:36pm Directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor attend the 'NAZA' screening at the Venice Film Festival on September 10, 2026. Carlo Paloni/Getty Images The International Documentary Association is coming to the defense of NAZA filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor . The nonprofit organization posted a letter to its website urging the Israeli government to stop what the IDA terms a “campaign of threats” against the directors, whose film is sharply critical of Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians. “IDA calls on the Israeli government to withdraw its threats against filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor,” the letter says. “We also call for an end to the public campaign of intimidation against them.” Related Stories Festivals NYFF Turns Up The Heat As 'Godzilla', 'Artificial', 'NAZA', 'You Can See Everything' Spark Festival Buzz News 'NAZA' Trailer: First Look At Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's Much-Talked-About Gaza Documentary The letter continues, “Since NAZA won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, senior Israeli officials have moved against its directors. The Culture Minister has accused them of treason and sought to revoke their citizenship. The Prime Minister has announced bills to revoke the citizenship of anyone who ‘slanders IDF soldiers’ and to raise defamation damages twentyfold.” (Read the full letter form the IDA below). Watch on Deadline ‘NAZA’ The Guardian/mk2 READ: ‘NAZA’ Review: Israeli Military Accused Of Depraved Indifference To Palestinian Life, Using AI To Kill In Gaza – Venice Film Festival The documentary, which holds its North American premiere Saturday at the New York Film Festival, is based on the account of 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers, who were interviewed at the height of Israeli military operations in Gaza. The military personnel, whose identities are concealed to protect their anonymity, describe callous disregard for Palestinian civilian life as the Israel Defense Forces pursued Hamas targets in the occupied territory. Whistleblowers allege the IDF set acceptable totals of civilian Palestinian deaths in attacks targeting suspected Hamas militants, in one case authorizing the killing of up to 500 civilians in pursuit of one target. The IDF, as Deadline has reported , has denied allegations in the film. The International Documentary Association writes, “The Israeli military disputes the film’s account, and it is entitled to do so. But as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Israel is bound by Article 19, under which restrictions on expression must be provided by law and be necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim. Revoking citizenship, imposing punitive damages, or opening security investigations in response to a documentary does not meet that test. The UN Human Rights Committee recognizes the protection of journalistic sources as part of freedom of expression, and the filmmakers’ right not to disclose the identities of their sources must be upheld.” The letter has gained more than 250 signatories so far, including from actors Javier Bardem and Mark Ruffalo, as well as many prominent figures in the documentary field including Oscar winners Laura Poitras, Rob Epstein, Dan Cogan, Alex Gibney, Roger Ross Williams, Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy, Orlando von Einsiedel, Dan Lindsay, and Ezra Edelman, and Oscar nominees Geeta Gandbhir, Liz Garbus, Connie Field, Guy Davidi, Rémi Grellety, Kellen Quinn, Joe Berlinger, Kirstine Barfod, Laura Nix, Sam Bisbee, Alexander Nanau, Joslyn Barnes, Raoul Peck, Kirby Dick, Amy Ziering, Carl Deal, and Tia Lessin, as well as former Sundance Film Festival director Tabitha Jackson, filmmakers Kirsten Johnson, Susan Lacy, Robert Bahar, Alison Klayman, Marjan Safinia, producer Ina Fichman, and many others. The IDA’s letter includes several bullet-pointed items: “IDA calls on the Government of Israel to: “withdraw the threats to revoke Abraham’s and Szor’s citizenship, and abandon the proposed legislation; “respect the filmmakers’ journalistic right to refuse to disclose the identities of confidential sources “reject changes to public film funding that penalize filmmakers for critical work or international recognition. “We also call on everyone taking part in the public debate to reject the intimidation of the filmmakers and their families.” Deadline has been alerted to a planned protest against NAZA outside Lincoln Center in New York City, where the film will screen on Saturday. According to organizers of the demonstration, they intend to “show documented footage from the October 7 massacre, alongside material challenging the film’s claims.” A nor’easter storm moving up the east coast may complicate any plans for an outdoor demonstration. Here’s the IDA letter, from the organization’s executive director, Dominic Asmall Willsdon . IDA calls on the Israeli government to withdraw its threats against filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. We also call for an end to the public campaign of intimidation against them. Since NAZA won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, senior Israeli officials have moved against its directors. The Culture Minister has accused them of treason and sought to revoke their citizenship. The Prime Minister has announced bills to revoke the citizenship of anyone who “slanders IDF soldiers” and to raise defamation damages twentyfold. This official rhetoric has been accompanied by a public campaign against the filmmakers. Graffiti branding them “traitors” has appeared, and protesters have gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents. Israeli filmmakers and human rights groups have warned that it could lead to violence. Disagreement with a film must not become a threat to the people who made it. The Israeli military disputes the film’s account, and it is entitled to do so. But as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Israel is bound by Article 19, under which restrictions on expression must be provided by law and be necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim. Revoking citizenship, imposing punitive damages, or opening security investigations in response to a documentary does not meet that test. The UN Human Rights Committee recognizes the protection of journalistic sources as part of freedom of expression, and the filmmakers’ right not to disclose the identities of their sources must be upheld. The Israel Film Council has also proposed ending credit for international festival selection in public film funding and creating a dedicated funding track for films celebrating IDF soldiers. Threats of this kind are a risk documentary makers face in the course of their work. More than 1,500 Israeli film professionals, 43 Israeli human rights organizations, and the directors of major international festivals have defended Abraham and Szor. IDA calls on the Government of Israel to: · withdraw the threats to revoke Abraham’s and Szor’s citizenship, and abandon the proposed legislation; · respect the filmmakers’ journalistic right to refuse to disclose the identities of confidential sources · reject changes to public film funding that penalize filmmakers for critical work or international recognition. We also call on everyone taking part in the public debate to reject the intimidation of the filmmakers and their families. We stand with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. title: What ‘60 Minutes’ Was Missing In Its First Two New Episodes, According to Its Ex-Managing Editor
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 25, 2026 4:49pm Norah O'Donnell on the Sept. 13 episode of '60 Minutes.' CBS News “I made a living for 34 years second-guessing everything I see or hear, so you have to take that into consideration.” That’s one of the first things that Guy Campanile, the famously exacting former managing editor of 60 Minutes and a 34-year veteran to CBS News , says to The Hollywood Reporter as he settles into an interview. At CBS News he was known for being ultra-frank even in a workplace that culturally encouraged vigorous debate as part of its story-honing process. (“It’s no secret at CBS News that I do not hold back. Many colleagues appreciated my directness. Some did not,” he wrote in an email to THR .) So he urges THR to take that into account as he offers his thoughts on the 59th season of 60 Minutes so far. His critiques are less stinging than one might assume given his previous assessment of why he and colleagues were fired from the program in May (that they refused to be “accomplices in the destruction of the most prestigious news program on American television”). Overall, Campanile echoes what at least a couple critics have said about the first episode of the 59th season: It didn’t seem much different than recent seasons of the program. “We kept hearing about a notebook full of ideas that the new executive producer had, and the broadcast had been described as a melting ice cube and that changes had to happen,” he says, adding that 60 Minutes also increased its viewership nine percent in the previous season. “And the broadcast I’ve seen the first few weeks, in the broad strokes, in shape and form, not in content, does not look very different. So I’m trying to understand why it was all blown up.” In May, Campanile’s time at CBS came to an abrupt end as he and multiple other staffers — including correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi, Cecilia Vega and senior program leaders Tanya Simon, Draggan Mihailovich and Matthew Polevoy — were ousted from the program. Correspondent Scott Pelley was also fired after a tense confrontation with an incoming leader about changes under CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss . The departures drew intense scrutiny as Weiss, who came up as an opinion journalist without traditional broadcast experience, was early in her tenure and some dismissed staffers alleged that under her leadership execs had attempted to interfere in their coverage for political reasons. Guy Campanile is a 34-year CBS veteran and was managing editor of 60 Minutes . Dave Kotinsky/Getty Images Within this context, Campanile’s biggest critique surrounds the marquee segment of the premiere, an interview with one of the U.S. Air Force officers shot down in Iran and rescued in a daring mission by the U.S. military. The segment struck Campanile as a fitting curtain-raiser to the new season, but the report also raised questions for him. “Where I, as a viewer, got stuck is how do we have the Secretary of Defense and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in that story and not ask about the conduct, the arc and the status of the war?” Campanile notes Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine, both interviewed in the piece, aren’t doing regular briefings on the status of the broadly unpopular war in Iran or many interviews with news outlets. “That made me go, huh, because among some viewers, they may see that as, boy, I guess they didn’t want to ask about the war because they wanted to get this interview with the [officer],” says Campanile. (He says that, during his time at the programs, conditions were never set by subjects for interviews at 60 Minutes ; correspondents could always ask what they wanted.) But CBS did air clips of correspondent Norah O’Donnell asking Hegseth what victory would look like in Iran and querying Caine on Iran’s missile capabilities on CBS Mornings . Her question to Caine about his concern over a munitions shortage also aired on Face the Nation — just not on 60 Minutes . Another Campanile critique: In its second episode of the season, 60 Minutes aired the first TV interview with Patrick Clancy, the ex-husband of Lindsay Clancy, a Massachusetts mother who murdered her three children. Clancy’s trial over the summer, which ended in a mistrial, captured global media attention and sparked conversation around postpartum mental illness, making the interview a huge get for 60 Minutes . But watching the segment, Campanile wondered what the larger purpose of the interview was. “I think it’s a high-interest story, just like the fighter pilot’s story was a high-interest story, but you have to bring more than just high interest, at least I believe that to be the case, because otherwise it feels a little tabloid-y,” he says. “And I don’t think that’s what people want from 60 Minutes . I just don’t. I think they want something more thoughtful.” The changes taking place at 60 Minutes and CBS News at large are all the more consequential now that the owner that ushered them in — Paramount Skydance — has settled a lawsuit with 12 state attorneys general to merge with Warner Bros. Discovery. WBD owns CNN, which if the transaction goes through could soon also be owned by Paramount Skydance. Campanile says he has “lots of concerns” about that prospect: “Chief among them is who is running this operation? Is it going to be Mark Thompson or is it going to be Bari Weiss?” He adds that it remains unclear to him how the editorial oversight board required by the settlement would work, given that specifics on the body haven’t been provided. “Much was made of the CBS News ombudsman. That guy’s been missing for a year,” Campanile says. Campanile is continuing to work in journalism, having just launched a media consultancy, FFWD Media Mentor, tailored to early-career and student journalists. The consultancy is geared toward professionals who aren’t receiving much guidance on the job; participants will likely receive some of that no-nonsense feedback Campanile was known for at 60 Minutes . When it comes to his former workplace, the former managing editor says he’s interested to see what the program does in the weeks ahead. “Maybe, maybe there is a secret sauce we didn’t understand, some kind of equation that we never contemplated,” he says of 60 Minutes . “And we’ll all find out together. The viewer has the final vote in all of this. I have said over and over again, you are what the scoreboard says you are… So let’s see where we are in April and March and May, and then the final verdict will come down.” THR

title: Dealmakers React To Paramount-WBD Settlement: “Tech Has Won”
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Shares In Barry Diller’s People Inc. Surge On Report Of Role-Reversal Acquisition Bid From MGM Resorts As Letterboxd Draws Interest From The New York Times, A24 And More, One Of Its Bankers Calls It “A Phenomenon” Dealmakers React To Paramount-WBD Settlement: “Tech Has Won” View All September 24, 2026 11:24am Story Arc Getty Images Mergers-and-acquisitions specialists weighed in Thursday on the Paramount -Warner Bros. Discovery merger, which appears just days from closing despite an 11th-hour legal hiccup. The $110 billion deal is on track to close in the coming days after a settlement of two antitrust lawsuits on Monday, though a federal judge delayed a hearing where she was due to review the settlement. Assuming it does finally close, the transaction “is evidence that, really, tech has won,” said David Hernand, a partner at the Simpson Thacher law firm, during a panel at the Financial Times Business of Entertainment Summit. “Tech came in and said, ‘We can build a better mousetrap on the distribution side.’ Distribution – when we’re talking about electronic distribution, whether it’s cable or internet – is moving atoms, and tech companies are really good at that, as it turns out.” Related Stories News Paramount To Move Its Class B Shares From Nasdaq To New York Stock Exchange In Early October Executives Shares In Barry Diller's People Inc. Surge On Report Of Role-Reversal Acquisition Bid From MGM Resorts Forced to go up against Apple, YouTube, Netflix, Amazon and others, Hernand added, “the traditional companies that relied on broadcast and cable as a form of distribution are trying to play catch-up and figure out how they’re going to play in this world.” Watch on Deadline Hernand’s firm is not involved in the Paramount deal, but two other panelists spoke from the perspective of stakeholders in the transaction. Aaron Sobel, a private equity partner at Apollo Global Management, which provided one-third of the financing for the merger, said it will give a traditional player a fighting chance against Big Tech. “I don’t think you can overstate how important getting that deal done was,” he said. “You had two companies that arguably couldn’t have existed without combining, and having someone like [Paramount CEO David Ellison] support the business is huge.” Prior to the merger, he added, “We were at a crossroads in the industry, where if that deal hadn’t gotten done … Netflix was gonna take over the world. Now, you’re seeing the pendulum really swing back to more traditional media, which is kind of ironic. And David is really betting on IP and what’s in that complex. So the fact that he’s the right owner for that and has the capital, obviously, to support that company, I don’t think you can overstate it.” Alex Michael, senior managing director and global head of sports and entertainment for LionTree, which advised Paramount on the merger, called it “a big deal, literally and figuratively… It was a big domino that everyone was waiting for, and I think it’ll be exciting to see where we go from here.” Sobel said the merger will have “so-many knock-on effects” in a positive way, across the theatrical movie business, distribution, production and “global movies and events.” Noting Hernand’s point, he said the deal was “against where the world was going. And I think there’s a lot of really exciting things that will come out of it.” Netflix, whose chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, spoke just prior to the panel, was the next topic. The streaming giant had agreed to acquire the studio and streaming business of WBD last December. After more than a dozen offers, Paramount finally managed to unseat Netflix with a richer offer for all of WBD. Netflix “kind of showed their hand by going after Warner Brothers, and with all due respect, look at their share price performance,” Sobel said. “The world knows what’s happening on engagement. If you don’t have really valuable IP, they’re going to shift to more traditional strategy over the next few years,” particularly with live events and sports. Noting that “what’s old is new again” for all players in media and entertainment, whether traditional or tech, he added, “I think a lot more of these companies are gonna look similar, not different.” Paramount-WBD is far from the last transaction set to reshape the industry. The panel wrapped with a provocative audience question from an NBCUniversal exec who asked the panel what the best path forward for her company would be. Comcast over the summer announced it plans to spin off NBCU, projecting the move will be completed by mid-2027. Hernand said the company should consider breaking up the portfolio “beyond what they’ve announced, meaning potentially separating NBC from Universal. “The more interesting move there would be combining Universal and Sony,” he added, acknowledging, “I know that would create a lot of outrage in Los Angeles.” Sobel noted that Comcast Co-CEO and Chairman Brian Roberts and his family control the company, and so-called “controlled companies” are often limited in terms of M&A. If Roberts is “open to be more flexible on how his vote works and his exposure to the business, it should be broken up,” Sobel said. “I would think Netflix and Comcast down the digital and the media side should probably come together at some point.” ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic ‘Mary Poppins’ TV Series In Works Digs Into More Complex Elements Of Novels Slew Of Hits Make It First Studio To Score $5 Billion Worldwide In 2026 More from this Story Arc Paramount WB September 25, 2026 Paramount To Move Its Class B Shares From Nasdaq To New York Stock Exchange In Early October September 25, 2026 ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition” View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments

title: ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition&#8221…
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition” Disney Legal Chief Warns Of “Hard Choices” & “Much Smaller Organization” Coming As Company Layoffs Loom No ParaBros Decision Today As Judge Delays Settlement Sign-Off; CA AG’s Office Insists Deal “Not The Result Of Collusion” View All September 25, 2026 1:07am Story Arc Paramount & Warner Bros water towers Getty Images “The Attorney General for the lead Plaintiff State, California, publicly criticized the very behavioral remedies that the parties now ask the Court to approve,”exclaims an amicus brief just filed in federal court by the Block the Merger coalition to take one last swing at stopping the antitrust settlement deal for Paramount ‘s $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros Discovery. Related Stories Executives Dealmakers React To Paramount-WBD Settlement: “Tech Has Won” News Paramount Moves Ahead With $7.5 Billion Debt Raise, Part Of Package To Finance WBD Acquisition “But whatever the reasons for the States’ about-face, neither time nor circumstance changes the fact that this merger lessens competition.” The September 21 announcement of an agreement between a dozen blue state AGs and David Ellison in the July-filed antitrust suit made it look like the $80 billion debt heavy ParaBros meld was finally and truly a done deal. However, with U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin Thursday granting 11th hour motions of objection by BTM and other Ellison foes and giving them until midnight on September 24 to file, closure has now been delayed. Watch on Deadline A delay, with Judge Martinez-Olguin also now pushing any settlement sign-off until at least noon on September 28 as Paramount responds to more concerns raised by Sen. Cory Booker (D-NJ), that could see Ellison having to begin paying that dreaded $7 million a day ticking fee to WBD shareholders starting October 1. A delay that Block the Merger, the League of United Latin American Citizens, and others make very evident they would like to see as permanent as possible. “The structure of the proposed consent decree puts Plaintiff States in the position of simultaneously representing two sets of stakeholders whose fundamental interests trade off,” BTM’s brief says. Noting, among a variety of critiques, that while guilds like the WGA have been promised nearly $18 million for their oversubscribed health plan ( AKA: “earmarked payments for tens of millions of dollars”) if the merger goes through, independent vendors and contractors will get almost nothing “That is precisely the kind of conflict that makes representation inadequate and a settlement procedurally unfair,” the coalition of the Free Press, the Committee for the First Amendment, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, the Future Film Coalition and the International Documentary Association argues in its hopes of convincing Judge Martinez-Olguin to “deny the Joint Motion to enter the proposed consent decree.” In their own brief filed in the midnight hour , LULAC and a group of Black pastors mine a similar vein as BTM – aka, CA AG Rob Bonta sold the industry out by buckling to Paramount’s leaked threats to leave the state and to pressure from ambitious Dems like Gavin Newsom to make a deal ASAP. Highlighting perceived shortcomings of the settlement deal and its granting of more power and reach to fatcats, LULAC says: “The proposed decree leaves that loss of independent decision-making largely intact. Its temporary film commitments measure releases and spending without preserving competition over which projects receive support. Its cable provisions regulate negotiations without preserving competition over the perspectives that are broadcast. And its news board, appointed by and reporting to the merged company, cannot replace the independent sources of programming the transaction eliminates. These defects concern the competitive harms the States pleaded, including diminished quality, variety, and viewpoints.” Due to the late hour, Paramount had nothing to say about these latest filings and the latest twist in their merger saga. Plus, the Ellison-run Paramount kinda said it all just after Block the Merger first filed their motion early Thursday to be granted the right to brief. “Any briefing and comment process that would enable non-parties to delay the closing of this transaction—inflicting massive harm on Paramount—without filing their own antitrust action, making the showing required under the Clayton Act to obtain preliminary injunctive relief, or posting a bond to protect Defendants from the harm caused by such delay would be improper,” Paramount said in its own (unsuccessful) opposition to BTM’s briefing wishes. I’ll get you a ruling in due course,” Judge Martinez-Olguin promised today in a virtual hearing on the now paused settlement. Having to also push back against Sen. Booker’s proposal of an independent review of the deal and the settlement, due course could be either sooner or later for Paramount. ‘Endgame’ Reissue & Three Other Pics To Top $20M Each In Big Weekend Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic ‘Mary Poppins’ TV Series In Works Digs Into More Complex Elements Of Novels Slew Of Hits Make It First Studio To Score $5 Billion Worldwide In 2026 More from this Story Arc Paramount WB September 25, 2026 Paramount To Move Its Class B Shares From Nasdaq To New York Stock Exchange In Early October September 24, 2026 David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi As CEO’s Soon-To-Be Owned CNN Banned From White House Event View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments

title: $110 billion merger
full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill NYFF Turns Up The Heat As ‘Godzilla’, ‘Artificial’, ‘NAZA’, ‘You Can See Everything’ Spark Festival Buzz From ‘Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty!’ To ‘The Stunt Driver’ & Mahershala Ali: Inside This Weekend’s New Indie Releases – Specialty Preview As Letterboxd Draws Interest From The New York Times, A24 And More, One Of Its Bankers Calls It “A Phenomenon” View All February 27, 2026 1:37pm Story Arc David Ellison Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures It’s official. For real this time. Warner Bros. Discovery is selling itself to Paramount for $31 a share in cash in a deal worth $110 billion. The companies unveiled their formal agreement on Friday. Paramount will hold a conference call and webcast on Monday at 8:30am ET to discuss the deal. Related Stories News David Zaslav Tries To Sell Paramount Deal To Shocked & Disappointed Employees At Town Hall: “We’re The Envy Of All Of The Industry” Executives Is Paramount’s Debt-Laden WBD Takeover Another Ill-Starred Hollywood Sequel? The formal announcement comes after WBD jilted Netflix, saying it received a Superior Proposal from the David Ellison company. Netflix had four days to match but declined immediately and walked away, leaving Par triumphant after a months-long hostile takeover attempt to pry apart its rivals. Paramount said the merged company is committed to producing a minimum of 30 theatrical films annually — 15 per studio per year. It promised film will receive a full theatrical release, with a minimum 45-day window globally and the current industry standard home video window prior to availability on subscription streaming services. Doubts around Netflix’s ultimate commitment to theatrical and intermediate windows was a major concern fo exhibitors and many in the Hollywood community. Watch on Deadline The merger is expected to close in the third quarter of 2026, subject regulatory clearances and approval by WBD shareholders, with a vote expected in the early spring. Paramount expects over $6 billion in cost synergies, short for cost savings. It cited a “combination of: technology integration (such as migrating the combined company to a single enterprise resource planning system and consolidating streaming technology stacks), corporate-wide efficiencies, including procurement savings, optimizing the combined real estate footprint, and otherwise streamlining operational efficiencies.” Many industry players anticipate thousands of layoffs. The transaction is funded by $47 billion in equity fully backed by the Ellison Family and RedBird Capital Partners. At closing, the equity may include other strategic and financial partners. Paramount did not name them but its previous hostile tender offer included backing from the Public Investment Fund (Kingdom of Saudi Arabia), L’imad Holding Company PJSC (Abu Dhabi) and Qatar Investment Authority (Qatar). Affinity Partners, the investment fund of President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner , had also been involved but withdrew. Ditto for China’s Tencent. Under the terms of the equity commitments, new shares of Class B Paramount stock will be issued at a price of $16.02 per share. In addition to the new cash equity investment, the transaction is backed by $54 billion of debt commitments from Bank of America, Citigroup, and Apollo, which includes $15 billion to backstop WBD’s existing bridge facility and $39 billion of incremental new debt. The $54 billion excludes $3.5 billion of bridge financing from these institutions to backstop an existing $3.5 billion revolving credit facility. The combined company will own a film library of more than 15,000 titles and thousands of hours of television programming with franchises including Harry Potter , Mission Impossible , Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones, the DC Universe, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles , Transformers, Star Trek and SpongeBob SquarePants . Combined sports rights will include the NFL, Olympics, UFC, PGA Tour, NHL, Big Ten and Big 12 Football, NCAA College Basketball, and Champions League, with the ability to distribute these rights collectively across all of its platforms. The merged company will have a massive portfolio of cable networks. That will include CNN, to the alarm of some lawmakers and many in the news business given shifts at CBS since David Ellison acquired control. The new company will inherit a diverse international portfolio from the former Discovery Communications, present in over 200 countries and territories with cable and free-to-air networks. Ellison, the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, has stressed technology and today’s announcement promised streamlining of “the technological underpinning of every aspect of the combined company’s businesses.” Paramount said it will be well-positioned to invest in growth, noting marquee deals since the Skydance merger with Trey Parker and Matt Stone of South Park , the UFC, the Duffer Brothers and Activision. However, Wall Streeters have noted it will carry a huge amount of debt that may constrain investment. “From the very beginning, our pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery has been guided by a clear purpose: to honor the legacy of two iconic companies while accelerating our vision of building a next-generation media and entertainment company. By bringing together these world-class studios, our complementary streaming platforms, and the extraordinary talent behind them, we will create even greater value for audiences, partners and shareholders — and we couldn’t be more excited for what’s ahead,” said Paramount CEO David Ellison. “I’m very pleased with the outcome we achieved for WBD shareholders and the entertainment industry. Our guiding principle throughout this process has been to secure a transaction that maximizes the value of our iconic assets and our century-old studio while delivering as much certainty as possible for our investors. title: still-pending
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition” Disney Legal Chief Warns Of “Hard Choices” & “Much Smaller Organization” Coming As Company Layoffs Loom David Ellison Dines With Trump & Xi As CEO’s Soon-To-Be Owned CNN Banned From White House Event View All September 24, 2026 12:12pm Story Arc L-R: Rob Bonta, Leticia James and David Ellison Getty Images Although David Ellison has given a lot of money to Democrats over the years, the Paramount CEO is probably not donating a dime to Sen. Cory Booker ‘s next campaign. The much disparaged state Attorneys General-negotiated settlement in Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery did not receive the court approval Thursday for which Rob Bonta and Ellison had hoped. Related Stories News Cory Booker Slams Paramount-WBD Merger Settlement But Blames Company And DOJ, Not State AGs News Block The Merger Coalition Asks Judge To Give Them Time To Formally Oppose Settlement Of Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger Lawsuit Instead, with briefs expected by midnight tonight from opponents of the mega-merger and Paramount moving ahead with a $7.5 billon debt raise, Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin told the assembled attorneys in a hearing today that she wanted them to address by September 29 concerns raised against the deal earlier Wednesday by longtime merger foe Booker (D-NJ). Stressing “I’ll get you a ruling in due course” (and probably stressing out Ellison as a $7 million-a-day ticking fee looms beginning October 1), the U.S. District judge also had some questions today – a lot of questions. Watch on Deadline Addressing a screen full of top firm lawyers and state AG officials during the virtual hearing, Martinez-Olguin wanted to know if the settlement and the consent decree actually “addresses the Clayton Act concerns” that were in the July 13 antitrust suit Bonta, New York’s Letitia James, and 10 other blue-state AGs filed against the merger. With the sharp realpolitiks at play from California Gov. Gavin Newsom and others for a settlement, Martinez-Olguin also had concerns that the roller-coaster deal was “not the result of collusion and was more of an arm’s length process.” Her blunt words clearly landed hard with her immediate audience of attorneys (and maybe the more than 640 others on the Zoom). Even before the judge issued her “homework” for the lawyers, the California Senior Assistant AG Paula Blizzard argued for the settlement while at the same time dismissing Paramount’s “threats” and “blackmail” to “pull out of California.” However, claiming the states were still prepared to take the whole matter to trial starting March 2, 2027 if the consent degree wasn’t approved, Blizzard also acknowledged the backlash the settlement has received over the past 72 hours since it was unveiled on Monday morning. “We absolutely recognize that this merger has engendered a large amount of controversy and commentary and feelings and concerns on a whole host of issues,” she said near the end of the nearly one-hour session. “A lot of these are outside antitrust,” Blizzard added. “They reflect the country’s very broad political and philosophical divides, concerns about the state of the news media, people’s relationship to big companies and consolidation and corporate power, and we hear those voices, we listen to those voices, we respect those voices. But at the end of the day, this is an antitrust case, and it is focused on the antitrust law.” Sen. Cory Booker Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Booker’s six-page letter to the judge Wednesday asked for her to “subject the proposed consent decree to an independent public-interest review before entering it.” Paramount filed paperwork of its own Wednesday, just before the virtual hearing, essentially telling the Garden State senator to mind his own business. During today’s hearing, Blizzard appeared to address Booker’s concerns without saying his name. Insisted the deal was “presumptively valid,” she told Martinez-Olguin it was the result of a final surge of talks over “tens of hours, in-person video conferences, phone conferences, drafts-all the normal things you would see in a consent decree, except magnified because you had 12 attorneys general on our side.” It should be noted, New Jersey was one of the states in the ParaBros antitrust gang, and their AG Jennifer Davenport agreed to the settlement announced September 21. The iconic gates of Paramount Pictures Mark Davis/Getty Images Aware his bosses were watching, Paramount outside counsel Josh Holiann made a point of disputing the use of the term ” blackmail” when it came to timed leaks the Ellisons were serious about pulling up Melrose lot stakes, jobs and productions to redder jurisdictions (“It was a business decision …Paramount had to make.”). In a less defensive posture, the Latham & Watkins attorney also promised the judge the penalties in the settlement would now “keep our feet to the fire.” Still, With Para and WBD lawyers Holian, Beth Wilkinson, Jeffrey Kessler, Daniel Petrocelli and Marguerite Sullivan on-screen (some clearly working on something else), it was mainly Blizzard who took point trying to sell Martinez-Olguin on the deal — and it sure seemed like a hard sell. “We believe we have five years of remedies that will remove the competitive concerns we see the harms we see and preserve competition,” Blizzard said. With nodded agreement from Paramount attorneys, Blizzard stressed the divestment of some cable channels if necessary and Miramax and other clauses in the settlement is “the best solution” other than blocking “it completely?” Sounding very much like she was arguing for Paramount, Blizzard ventured into some hard Hollywood realities to give the deal context. “Obviously, in this case, Warner Bros originally said it was going to sell its assets,” Blizzard said. “So, if we block this merger, there will probably be another one, perhaps before Your Honor, in a year or so, and is that the best solution for the markets to preserve the competition that the Clayton Act requested.” Kneecapped to some extent by Zoom-wide technical glitches that initially prevented some of the attorneys and state government officials from participating in the virtual hearing, the hearing on the now delayed settlement sign-off was delayed itself by nearly 15 minutes. Now, with that ticking fee clock ticking, ParaBros closure is also once again delayed — at least until Monday at noon. Well played Sen. full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘Gilded Age’ Christmas Album To Feature Carrie Coon, Laura Benanti, Audra McDonald, Adrienne Warren & Other Cast Members And Broadway Stars Global Citizen, All Things Go & CBGB Festivals Canceled Due To Extreme Weather Threat For New York City Ed Sheeran’s Controversial Gillette Stadium Concerts Canceled As Boston Braces For Nor’easter View All September 25, 2026 8:28am Ed Sheeran in Boston, 2025 Paras Griffin/Getty Images for for iHeartRadio Ed Sheeran ‘s beleaguered Gillette Stadium concerts tonight and Saturday have been canceled due to the nor’easter threatening New England with severe weather . In an Instagram post, Messina Touring – the promotor of Sheeran’s tour – wrote, “Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England through the weekend anf following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium. Related Stories News Macklemore Launches Free Palestine Tour; U.S. Dates To Be Announced News Global Citizen & All Things Go Festivals Canceled Due To Extreme Weather Threat For New York City “The decision,” the statement continues, “was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.” Local weather reports for Foxborough, Massachusetts – the Boston-area town where Gillette Stadium is located – are predicting up to 2 inches of rain and 40 MPH wind gusts from the nor’easter. Watch on Deadline Messina Touring said refunds are available at points of purchase, and ticketholders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded. The nor’easter is just the latest storm to impact Sheeran’s Loop tour : After Sheeran, under pressure from billionaire Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, fired opening act Macklemore for pro-Palestine statements made at a previous concert, a storm of controversy and backlash engulfed Sheeran and the tour. Other acts and musicians on the tour resigned in protest, forcing Sheeran to apologize and attempt to explain his actions. Macklemore subsequently announced that he would launch his own “Free Palestine” tour, with proceeds going to various charities supporting the Palestinian people.
